identifiers.title: Sweet/dessert foods are more appealing to adolescents after sleep restriction
identifiers.authors: Simon SL, Field J, Miller LE, DiFrancesco M, Beebe DW
identifiers.citation: Simon SL, Field J, Miller LE, DiFrancesco M, Beebe DW. Sweet/dessert foods are more appealing to adolescents after sleep restriction. PLoS One. 2015;10(2):e0115434. doi:10.1371/journal.pone.0115434

sampleSize.quote: Of 38 teens randomized to the sleep manipulation, one dropped out and 6 were non-adherent to the sleep protocol (defined as <60 minutes difference in average sleep duration across the SR and HS conditions), leaving a final sample of 31 (59% female, 52% Caucasian, 41% African-American, mean age 15.7 ± 1.0 years).

facts.label: Length of the whole protocol
facts.quote: The three-week protocol consisted of a baseline week, followed randomly by five consecutive nights of SR (6.5 hours in bed) versus healthy sleep duration (HS; 10 hours in bed), a 2-night wash-out period, and a 5-night cross-over.

facts.label: Short-sleep nights: 6.5 hours in bed
facts.quote: The three-week protocol consisted of a baseline week, followed randomly by five consecutive nights of SR (6.5 hours in bed) versus healthy sleep duration (HS; 10 hours in bed), a 2-night wash-out period, and a 5-night cross-over.

facts.label: Healthy-sleep nights: 10 hours in bed
facts.quote: The three-week protocol consisted of a baseline week, followed randomly by five consecutive nights of SR (6.5 hours in bed) versus healthy sleep duration (HS; 10 hours in bed), a 2-night wash-out period, and a 5-night cross-over.

facts.label: Each condition lasted five nights in a row
facts.quote: The three-week protocol consisted of a baseline week, followed randomly by five consecutive nights of SR (6.5 hours in bed) versus healthy sleep duration (HS; 10 hours in bed), a 2-night wash-out period, and a 5-night cross-over.

facts.label: Two normal nights between the conditions
facts.quote: The three-week protocol consisted of a baseline week, followed randomly by five consecutive nights of SR (6.5 hours in bed) versus healthy sleep duration (HS; 10 hours in bed), a 2-night wash-out period, and a 5-night cross-over.

facts.label: A random draw set which condition came first
facts.value: randomized to an order of the experimental conditions
facts.quote: Adolescents who successfully completed the baseline week were randomized to an order of the experimental conditions (SR first vs. HS first) in a counterbalanced, within-subjects crossover design.

facts.label: A first week with bedtimes of their own choosing, to settle the body clock
facts.quote: Teens’ circadian phase was first stabilized in a baseline week, during which they could self-select their bedtimes, but were asked to consistently awaken at a time that would allow them to come in to our office for an 8:30 AM appointment/visit.

facts.label: Same wake time every morning, weekends included
facts.value: subjects were not allowed to “sleep in” any morning during the study
facts.quote: That wake time was maintained throughout the study (i.e., subjects were not allowed to “sleep in” any morning during the study, including the weekends) to minimize shifts in circadian rhythm.

facts.label: Only the bedtime moved to set the hours in bed
facts.value: bedtimes were adjusted to allow 6.5 hours in bed each night for 5 nights
facts.quote: When in the SR condition, teens’ bedtimes were adjusted to allow 6.5 hours in bed each night for 5 nights.

facts.label: No naps; caffeine capped at 1 coffee or energy drink a day
facts.value: no more than 1 coffee or energy drink per day
facts.quote: Teens were asked to refrain from napping and limit caffeine intake to no more than 1 coffee or energy drink per day or no more than 2 caffeinated sodas per day.

facts.label: All sleep happened at home
facts.quote: All sleep occurred at home and was monitored via a daily sleep diary and actigraphy (MicroMotionlogger Sleep Watch, Ambulatory Monitoring, Inc.).

facts.label: Sleep checked with a wrist motion sensor and a sleep diary
facts.value: a daily sleep diary and actigraphy
facts.quote: All sleep occurred at home and was monitored via a daily sleep diary and actigraphy (MicroMotionlogger Sleep Watch, Ambulatory Monitoring, Inc.).

facts.label: Tests on the Saturday morning after each condition
facts.value: Assessments were conducted on Saturday mornings after each experimental condition
facts.quote: Assessments were conducted on Saturday mornings after each experimental condition.

facts.label: 84 food photos per visit: 42 sweets and desserts, 42 other foods
facts.quote: Two matched sets with 84 photos of 42 sweets/desserts and 42 non-sweets (fruits/vegetables, meat/eggs) were compiled. One set was viewed at each experimental week visit and teens were asked to rate how appetizing each picture looked on a 1–4 scale (“gross,” “OK,” “good,” “delicious”).

facts.label: Each photo rated 1 to 4, from “gross” to “delicious”
facts.quote: Two matched sets with 84 photos of 42 sweets/desserts and 42 non-sweets (fruits/vegetables, meat/eggs) were compiled. One set was viewed at each experimental week visit and teens were asked to rate how appetizing each picture looked on a 1–4 scale (“gross,” “OK,” “good,” “delicious”).

facts.label: Main outcome: how appealing the food photos looked
facts.value: The primary outcomes for this study were obtained via a computerized food-appeal rating-system
facts.quote: The primary outcomes for this study were obtained via a computerized food-appeal rating-system.

facts.label: Ratings were consistent from one visit to the next
facts.quote: Each teen’s mean rating was computed for each food type (sweets, non-sweets) within each condition (SR and HS), yielding composites with high test-retest reliability (r = .79-.83).

facts.label: Hunger rated on a 4-point scale
facts.quote: Teens rated their hunger on a 4-point scale from “not hungry” to “very hungry” immediately after the food-appeal ratings.

facts.label: Food eaten was an exploratory check, in about three quarters of the teens
facts.value: roughly 3/4 of the sample also underwent a 24-hour diet recall
facts.quote: To allow for exploratory comparison against our prior dietary findings, roughly 3/4 of the sample also underwent a 24-hour diet recall at each experimental week assessment visit using the USDA Multiple Pass Method [].

facts.label: The diet interview asked about the day before (the last short or healthy night's day)
facts.value: asked about dietary intake the previous day
facts.quote: There was no apparent relationship between time of the interview and our dietary outcomes, probably because all interviews were conducted during a narrow time window, and asked about dietary intake the previous day (i.e., interviews conducted Saturday morning asked about food intake Friday).

facts.label: Teens who strongly disliked a food type were left out of that analysis
facts.value: subjects who indicated a strong dislike (mean rating <2) of a particular food type were removed from that analysis
facts.quote: For the food appeal analyses, subjects who indicated a strong dislike (mean rating <2) of a particular food type were removed from that analysis.

facts.label: No sign that the first condition carried over into the second
facts.value: No significant interaction was found across any of our outcome measures (all p > .05)
facts.quote: No significant interaction was found across any of our outcome measures (all p > .05), indicating that the effect of sleep manipulation did not vary based on the order in which HS or SR was presented.
facts.outcome: Carry-over between conditions

facts.label: Who could join: typically developing 14 to 17 year-olds
facts.value: typically-developing 14–17 year-olds without a current psychiatric diagnosis
facts.quote: Similar to our prior study [], we enrolled typically-developing 14–17 year-olds without a current psychiatric diagnosis or history of neurological illness/injury.

facts.label: Excluded: marked obesity (BMI over 30) or intellectual disability
facts.quote: In addition, we excluded for intellectual disability or marked obesity (IQ<70 or BMI>30, initially screened by parent and teen report, then confirmed objectively during a baseline visit).

facts.label: Recruited by flyers in a regional care network and a clinic for low-income families
facts.value: flyers posted throughout a regional care network
facts.quote: Participants were recruited from flyers posted throughout a regional care network and, to help ensure representation of underserved populations, research staff were available to answer questions in an adolescent health clinic that tends to serve low-income families.

facts.label: Approved by the hospital's ethics board; teens and parents agreed in writing
facts.value: approved by the Institutional Review Board
facts.quote: All procedures were approved by the Institutional Review Board at Cincinnati Children’s Hospital Medical Center.

facts.label: Who paid for the study
facts.quote: This work was supported by the National Institutes of Health (R01 HL092149, UL1 RR026314).

facts.label: The funder had no role in the study
facts.quote: The funders had no role in study design, data collection and analysis, decision to publish, or preparation of the manuscript.

facts.label: Competing interests
facts.quote: Competing Interests: The authors have declared that no competing interests exist.
